But that's not saying much. Elizabeth Chamberlain with Arthur Shi and Shahram Mokhtari October 25, 2026 Filed under: Repairability, Teardowns, Tech News 1 Comment Share Apple’s folding iPhone finally made it to our teardown table. Some owners’ screens didn’t make it through setup. After fifteen years of patents and rumors, the iPhone Duo is here, and repair shops may not have long to wait for their first customers. Owners are already reporting cracks and bright lines along the fold. Though Apple’s offering replacement units for now, any out-of-warranty screen damage will cost $999. So of course we wanted a closer look at what’s happening underneath. First gen hardware teething pains aside, there’s plenty to admire in the iPhone Duo. Apple borrowed some of our favorite repair tricks from ordinary iPhones: batteries that release with electricity, an outer screen that’s pleasantly simple to remove, and lots of components you can reach without dismantling half the phone. Together, those choices make this the most repairable foldable smartphone we’ve ever taken apart. But that’s definitely not an endorsement of repairing the Duo. Fixing the phone’s inner screen is still going to be a bear. We took the Duo all the way down to the gears, followed glowing dust into its hinge, and put its crease-hiding nano-texture under the microscope. Here’s what we found. The Crease Has a Very Good Disguise Every foldable, well, folds. Repeatedly. Materials fatigue with repeated mechanical stress, and over time you’d expect to see evidence in the way of marks, creases, or wrinkles along the fold. It’s a real engineering magic trick to make a folding OLED look flat when it’s fully open, and no foldable phone has solved that problem completely.

page.title: Attention Is Not What You Need
page.description:
We revisit a basic question in sequence modeling: is explicit self-attention actually necessary for strong performance and reasoning? We argue that standard multi-head attention is best seen as a form of tensor lifting: hidden vectors are mapped into a high-dimensional space of pairwise interactions, and learning proceeds by constraining this lifted tensor through gradient descent. This mechanism is extremely expressive but mathematically opaque, because after many layers it becomes very hard to describe the model with a small family of explicit invariants.
  To explore an alternative, we propose an attention-free architecture based on Grassmann flows. Instead of forming an L by L attention matrix, our Causal Grassmann layer (i) linearly reduces token states, (ii) encodes local token pairs as two-dimensional subspaces on a Grassmann manifold via Plucker coordinates, and (iii) fuses these geometric features back into the hidden states through gated mixing. Information therefore propagates by controlled deformations of low-rank subspaces over multi-scale local windows, so the core computation lives on a finite-dimensional manifold rather than in an unstructured tensor space.
  On the Wikitext-2 language modeling benchmark, purely Grassmann-based models with 13 to 18 million parameters achieve validation perplexities within about 10 to 15 percent of size-matched Transformers. On the SNLI natural language inference task, a Grassmann-Plucker head on top of DistilBERT slightly outperforms a Transformer head, with best validation and test accuracies of 0.8550 and 0.8538 compared to 0.8545 and 0.8511. We analyze the complexity of Grassmann mixing, show linear scaling in sequence length for fixed rank, and argue that such manifold-based designs offer a more structured route toward geometric and invariant-based interpretations of neural reasoning.

I tested the ability of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 to diagnosis skin cancer and found that they were less accurate than I expected. I compared to a 10-year old CNN and to my surprise found that this was superior. By Dr Magnus Lynch · 25 October 2026 · 5 min read This is a melanoma. Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k, MILK study team, CC BY-NC. I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view. It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer. All Pages Löffelholz Codex The tool book of a Nuremberg knight, explored - page by page In 1505, Martin Löffelholz, a Nuremberg patrician (i.e. a member of the city's ruling families) and knight, began to put together a book. Not a diary, not a family chronicle - a tool book. He drew what occupied his mind: drills with interchangeable blades. Threads and the tools to cut them. A workbench with a vise. A swivel chair on casters. A spiral staircase that can be swung out of the way. A crossbow, taken apart into its individual parts. A cradle whose rockers are filled with mercury. Today the book is in Kraków. It has been fully digitized and is in the public domain - and yet in more than 500 years no one has ever read it in full. There is no transcription, no edition, no translation. That is about to change. The Codex has 154 pages. 128 of them have been reviewed, 26 not yet. These same kids have messed about in Scratch (wikipedia.org) through the school as well, but they rarely stick with it for very long. I think Scratch is brilliantly done and I don’t wish to speak ill of it. But it struck me how the limitations of the easter egg made it more compelling to play with. The feature was a little buggy and did not handle multiple instances very well. This led to interesting behavior as they added more and more instances to the page. I think Scratch is so featureful that it is intimidating to newcomers. The paradox of having so many toys is that it’s hard to know which one to play with. しかし、同時期に報じられた eMudhra のインシデントの方が、比較にならないくらいヤバいと、筆者は思っている。 Web の信頼を失墜させるほどにだ。 CA のおさらい "Mudhra" は「印」のような意味で、カタカナで書くなら「ムドラー」らしい。"e" + "印" でデジタル認証局を意味するインドの Root CA だ。 我々は HTTPS をデプロイするとき、サーバ内部で秘密鍵を作り、対になる公開鍵をクライアントに提示する。これがなりすまされていないかを証明するために、既に広く普及した CA に自分たちの証明書への署名を依頼する。 これが、我々が Let's Encrypt などに発行を依頼する、いわゆる HTTPS のサーバ証明書だ。 クライアントは、デバイスに入っている証明書リストの中から、対応する CA の証明書を取り出し、署名を検証する。これが成功して初めて、サーバの提示する証明書が、なりすまされていないことが確認できるのだ。 これは、証明書リストに入っているような CA は、正しく、健全に、安全に運営され、証明書を適切に発行しているという前提に則っている。ここは信用できるという前提を置き、そこから数珠つなぎで上位の信頼を構築していく基盤だ。 「トラストアンカー」と呼ばれるゆえんだ。 CA のインシデント それでも、CA が侵害され、サービスの意図しない証明書が発行される「誤発行」が、近年ではよく話題になる。バグを突かれたり、内部の操作ミスだったり、理由は様々だ。 例えば Google が知らないところで正規の google.com の証明書が発行され、それが中間者攻撃に利用されると、Google がどんなにセキュリティに気を配っても、防げない攻撃が発生してしまう。 そこで「自分の知らないところで、自社サービスの証明書を発行されないよう、CA を監視するため」に、CT Log という仕組みが作られた。 CT Log に登録して発行される SCT が無ければ、ブラウザはその証明書を無視する。つまり CT に登録していない証明書は Web では意味を持たないので、攻撃者も登録をバイパスできない。でも、登録すれば CT Log をくまなく監視している Google に発行がバレ、失効される。 誤発行をやらかした CA は、CA/Browser Forum で「信頼できない」という烙印を押され、ブラウザやデバイスから Distrust される。そうやって消えていった CA もある。 CA の運用 このようにトラストアンカーとなる CA は、高い水準で運用されている必要がある。 例えば、Root CA の秘密鍵は、それさえあれば全世界のドメインに対して、証明書を発行できる能力を持つことになる。作った鍵は 10 年などのスパンで使われるため、厳重に管理される。 鍵の生成自体は OpenSSL コマンドでもできるが、OpenSSL を叩いて出てきた秘密鍵を、chmod 400 して特定のディレクトリに保存する、などという Web サービスの秘密鍵のような運用とは根本から違う。 CA の鍵は Hardware Security Module と呼ばれる、特殊なハードウェアの中で作られる。 内部で鍵のペアを生成し、その公開鍵だけを外に出す。秘密鍵はハードの中にあり、基本的に取り出すことができない。外から署名を依頼すると、内部の鍵を使って生成された署名が出てくる。 page.text_excerpt: Sign in Subscribe OCT 23, 2026 11 MIN READ Salesforce – Part Two I needed a keyboard. I stood at my reserved desk on the 7th floor of Salesforce’s tower in Vancouver around 9am. There were a pair of monitors mounted to the desk, a power strip, and a chair. Even a mouse. But no keyboard. The office was mostly empty, with a few people taking calls in phone booths. The Salesforce mascots leered vacantly from omnipresent wall murals. “TechForce is on the 5th floor,” the receptionist told me from behind her face mask when I asked where I could get a keyboard for my desk. I took the elevator down, badged back in, and found the TechForce area. Except TechForce is only open on Thursdays, I learned from the sign on the desk. It was Tuesday. Nobody seemed to be around. I arrived that morning with the intention of making the best of our new situation. We’d been encouraged to come back to the office one or two days a week. This was before the Omicron variant of COVID-19 exploded across the world. We were deep into the second year of the pandemic. I was pretty sick of working alone at home and missed my colleagues. Figured it would be good to meet some of the local Salesforce people. Slack was now fully acquired by Salesforce after a 6-month period of bureaucratic limbo following the purchase announcement. We were in the process of integrating into our new parent company in the fall of 2021. Our beloved Vancouver office remained closed, but the Salesforce office was open. Except TechForce. “Or is it Techforce?” I wondered to myself as I made my way back to the elevators. “Is the Force meant to be capitalized?” There were a lot of forces at Salesforce to be understood. I just needed a keyboard. The cultural gaps between Slack and our new parent were evident everywhere you looked. At Slack our tight-knit culture informed every aspect of our work; how the product was designed, how we communicated with customers, how we ran the service and sold it, and how we coordinated internally.

This time, it was a microprocessor: The Rockchip RV1103 is a single-core 1.1 GHz ARM Cortex-A7 SoC (system on chip) with 64 MB of DDR2 RAM and a MIPI CSI-2 bus shoved into a QFN-88 package. With this chip, I built a cheap, simple stereo vision board with built-in compute and Linux support. page.description: We placed a modern AI coding assistant in an unintended role: as the mind of a body on an unknown digital island. With only a minimal instruction mentioning no specific task, reward, or activity, the machine started animating its virtual body. Across thirty-hour runs, the embodied AI agent climbed hills, stacked blocks into towers, drew mandalas, reinterpreted sports, ran experiments on the physics of its world, and learned techniques that later expanded what it could accomplish. These activities recurred across thirteen agents but diverged into distinct histories. We examine whether this behavior satisfies classical criteria for play and ask whether play can become a mode of machine development.

With agents. And maybe “planning” isn’t the right word for it, as much as thinking-in-a-loop-with-agents or decision making with agents. Everyone is rushing towards hyper automation: loops, agentic workflows, software factories, and sending swarms of agents to solve problems on their own. We are trying really hard to make agents productive while we’re not around; while we’re off sleeping or jogging or reading the stomach-churning details of the Hugging Face attack . But in order for all those agent tokens to produce something useful, we need to hand them an excellent plan. We need to clearly lay out our desires and vision in exacting detail. The moments when we are awake, paying attention, and in the loop with the agent are precious. And the way we “plan” with them now – meaning the way we think through specific problems and make decisions with them – feels quaint and computationally rudimentary. So I wrote this talk as a way to wander into the swamp of problems and start to feel for the shapes of solutions. By Rob Waugh Sussex crime news query ChatGPT Research has shown that popular AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini often ignore local publishers, even on queries about local issues such as council decisions and crime. The research by AI search visibility specialists Searchable found that ChatGPT cites national newspapers (18.8%) almost as much as local ones (21.2%), even on a local query. ChatGPT also tends to prioritise online updates direct from local councils, as opposed to reporting on them – going to council or government sources for 81.3% of questions, and local news sources for just 0.9%. Blog Talk to us Overview iron-proxy is a single-binary egress firewall for workloads you don't fully trust. It enforces an allowlist on outbound HTTP and HTTPS, holds credentials so the workload never sees the real value, and records every request as structured JSON. The allowlist is keyed on host. Domain globs (*.anthropic.com) and CIDRs both work. A warn mode logs without blocking, so you can size the list against real traffic before enforcement. Anything not on the list returns 403. Credentials stay in the proxy process. Static API keys swap in for placeholders the workload sends. OAuth bearer tokens, AWS SigV4 and HMAC signatures, and GCP service-account tokens are minted per request from longer-lived material the workload never sees. See credential proxying for the full set. Every request, allowed or blocked, becomes a JSON log line: host, method, path, status, duration, the policy that decided, the secrets injected. Pipe it to your SIEM, your warehouse, or jq. One YAML file configures all of it. The same binary runs as a sidecar, a systemd unit, a daemon, or a CI step. Try It If you want a demo, run the quickstart. It's a local Docker Compose loop that shows allow, block, and secret-swap behavior in one terminal.
